sections.h2: Marion County recorder's counter in Ocala
sections.html:
Official Records is in the Clerk of Court Annex Building at 19 N Pine Avenue, room 124, on the first floor in Ocala. The desk is open weekdays from 8:00 am to 5:00 pm and answers at 352-671-5630.

Mail goes to Clerk of Court and Comptroller, Attn: Recording, P.O. Box 1030, Ocala, FL 34478-1030. Overnight couriers use a different street address, 110 NW 1st Avenue, Ocala, FL 34475. Mixing the two up risks a missed delivery, because a courier cannot deliver to a post office box.

The Clerk is the county recorder, so one general series of Official Records books holds deeds, mortgages, liens, contracts, affidavits, plats, condominium declarations, bills of sale, judgments, military discharge certificates and declarations of domicile.

sections.h2: Can a deed be recorded without visiting the office?
sections.html:
Yes, through an approved e-recording vendor. The Clerk accepts submissions from CSC eRecording Solutions, eRecording Partners Network and Simplifile and does not recommend or endorse any of them. You need a computer, a scanner and internet access.

The Clerk presents the benefits as no check writing, no runner or mailing cost, and keeping the original document in your hands. Documents must come through one of those vendors; you cannot upload one straight to the Clerk.

Property Alert sends a notice when a document is recorded against a parcel or a name you register. The Clerk calls it the first step in protecting your property and says plainly that it does not prevent fraud. If an alert looks wrong, you have to contact law enforcement or take legal action.

  • Register a username and password, then confirm through the emailed link.
  • Find the Parcel ID on the Property Appraiser's site by owner name or site address.
  • Enter party names in index order, surname first, such as Smith John A or Smith John Jr.
  • Add several spellings, including middle names and initials, to cast a wider net.

Check the Official Records Search to see how names appeared on past recordings before deciding which variations to enter. Owners who split time elsewhere, such as snowbirds and landlords with out-of-state addresses, gain the most, since a fraudulent deed can sit unnoticed when nobody watches the mailbox. Heirs holding a parent's Ocala house should also register, using the decedent's name as well as their own.

sections.h2: Marion County offices that work with the Clerk
sections.html:
Three offices cover most of a property transaction: the Clerk records, the Property Appraiser values, and the Tax Collector bills. Each runs its own site with different tools.

Marion County offices and what each one offers
OfficeLocation and phoneUseful tools
Clerk, Official Records19 N Pine Ave, room 124, Ocala; 352-671-5630Search, e-recording, Property Alert
Property Appraiser501 SE 25th Avenue, Ocala; (352) 368-8300Property and sales search, Map It+, homestead e-file, tax estimator, TRIM notice, value adjustment board
Tax Collector(352) 368-8200Pay online, installment plan, deferred taxes, tax deed applications, tourist tax

The appraiser takes walk-ins or appointments and offers a mortgage estimate letter, a mailing address change request and links for reporting homestead fraud or property damage. The 2026 real estate, tangible personal property and railroad rolls are open for collection at the Tax Collector.

sections.h2: How Marion County recording charges are built
sections.html:
Fees follow the schedule in section 28.24 of the Florida Statutes: one amount for the first sheet, a smaller one for each additional sheet, a modest charge for names beyond the fourth, and separate per-sheet trust fund and technology add-ons. Plats and tax deed applications have their own lines. Ask the Official Records desk for a total before you send a check.

Deeds also draw documentary stamp tax under section 201.02, calculated on the consideration, which includes any mortgage tied to the property. All signers are liable no matter who agrees to pay, and the Clerk gathers the tax at recording.

sections.h2: Why search Official Records before you sell?
sections.html:
The search shows what a buyer's title agent will find. A recorded lien, an old mortgage with no release or a stray affidavit can hold up a closing, and each is easier to fix before a contract exists.

  • Search your own name in every form you have used.
  • Check the parcel for recorded declarations that bind the lot.
  • Match the legal description on your last deed to the one you plan to sign.
  • Sign deeds before two witnesses, which Florida requires for a conveyance of land.

If the search turns up something unfamiliar, ask the title company or an attorney what it means before you list. An item that is cleared early rarely becomes a surprise later.

Tax deed sales run online. The Clerk says they are open to the public, held through the RealAuction platform, and scheduled once or twice a month on Wednesdays starting at 9:00 a.m. Separately, the Tax Collector's site has an online tax deed application and a way to buy county-held certificates.

The timing is the lesson for a seller. Unpaid taxes can move a parcel from a bill to a certificate to a public sale, and a recorded tax deed will show up in Official Records. Clear any open balance with the Tax Collector at (352) 368-8200 before it gets that far. Installment and deferral options appear as separate pages on the Tax Collector's menu.

sections.h2: What the Property Appraiser's site offers buyers and sellers
sections.html:
The appraiser's home page links a property search, a Map It+ tool, a sales search and a property tax estimator, plus an e-file form for homestead exemption and for tangible personal property returns. It also has a TRIM notice page, the Value Adjustment Board, a code list and a frequently asked questions page with important dates.

  • Use the sales search to see what nearby homes recorded.
  • Use the estimator to test a purchase price, since a sale resets assessed value for most homes.
  • Request a mortgage estimate letter if a lender asks for tax figures.
  • Report suspected homestead fraud through the link on the home page.

sections.h2: Preparing a deed for a Marion County sale
sections.html:
1. Copy the legal description exactly from your current deed.
  2. Confirm how each seller's name is written in the record and match it on the new deed.
  3. Arrange two witnesses and a notary for signing.
  4. Ask the title company whether it will e-record through a vendor or whether you must deliver the original.
  5. Request a total from the Official Records desk if you are mailing a check.

After signing, keep your own copy and watch for the recorded image to appear in the Official Records Search. If it does not show up when the title company said it would, call the Official Records desk and ask where the filing stands.

A cash buyer skips lender underwriting, which leaves recording and title items as the main pieces still to finish. Getting them right the first time keeps the closing date.

faqs.q: Which Marion County desk takes a deed for the record?
faqs.a: The Clerk's Official Records department at 19 N Pine Avenue, room 124, in Ocala, or an approved e-recording vendor.

faqs.q: What is the mailing address for Marion County recording?
faqs.a: Clerk of Court and Comptroller, Attn: Recording, P.O. Box 1030, Ocala, FL 34478-1030. Overnight couriers use 110 NW 1st Avenue, Ocala, FL 34475.

faqs.q: Which vendors does Marion County accept for e-recording?
faqs.a: CSC eRecording Solutions, eRecording Partners Network and Simplifile. The Clerk does not endorse any of them.

faqs.q: Does Property Alert stop property fraud?
faqs.a: No. It only tells you when a matching document is recorded. If an alert looks unauthorized, contact law enforcement or take legal action.

faqs.q: Who values my Marion County home?
faqs.a: The Property Appraiser, at 501 SE 25th Avenue in Ocala, (352) 368-8300. The Tax Collector at (352) 368-8200 handles the bill.
